project_dependencies.use: Exact root 01.0001, vṛddhi, causative and result guards. PG377 is unprefixed present, not this Vedic text.
6.4.55 primary ām, its luk and the second word as independent finite carrier.
Inherited kṛ P third-plural perfect exponent cakruḥ.
Kāśikā 32105 preserves the separate Vedic past rule.
Existing masculine hotṛ dative singular hotre.
The two -yai datives and feminine āgnīdhrīyām accusative remain PG771’s.
PG14 full coefficient and native history algebra.

source_observations.observation: The prose places two formally dissimilar causal predicates on either side of quotation. All role terms and governing verbs are retained.

source_observations.locator: Sāyaṇa, Aitareya commentary, pañcikā 6, adhyāya 28, sixth khaṇḍa (6.14.2)
source_observations.observation: He assigns the recitation to the work performed by the agnīdhra. The explanation has both a dative paraphrase and the genitive of the activity. The digital OCR is damaged around the title.

source_observations.locator: Sāyaṇa, same section on 6.14.4, printed pp. 718–719 in the displayed text
source_observations.observation: His first explanation names the two priests and paraphrases the invitation with karavāma. The second names the activity of the agnīdhra, a particular additional verse and what the gods have done.
The first person of loṭ receives āṭ and pit status. Its vowel belongs to the finite ending.
Final s of first-person endings is lost under the ṅit rule, extended to the imperative by its laṅ-like operations.

source_observations.locator: Whitney, Sanskrit Grammar, chapter XIV, discussion of modal forms
source_observations.observation: Descriptive grammar includes subjunctive first persons in the imperative set. This general comparison does not determine a second parse specific to the transmitted Aitareya verse or prose.
Vedic liṭ has past reference without requiring the ordinary parokṣa condition of 3.2.115.
Affix-final primary verb admits ām in the non-mantra environment. The auxiliary has its own perfect endings.
Causal i takes ay before ām, which has a distinct source from the ending of the first-person proposal.
Auxiliary kṛ receives the voice of the primary in the specified ām construction. The R̥gvedic noun for the person is not its agreement controller.
